findings: Path traversal vulnerability: The anchors, identity_reference, and deliverable_set fields in WorkOrder (model.py:123-126) accept arbitrary path strings from JSON without validation. Since work orders can originate from external sources (github-issue), an attacker could inject paths like '../../etc/passwd' or '../../../sensitive/data'. While currently only used for display in packet_anchor_section (quality.py:131-143), these unvalidated paths persist in work order storage and could enable unauthorized file access if future code uses them for file operations. Mitigation: Add path validation in WorkOrder.from_dict to ensure paths are relative, within expected boundaries, and contain no traversal sequences.

Missing input validation in quality.py: Functions is_visual_run (line 48) and get_product_type (line 59) access work_order.surfaces and work_order.description without checking these attributes exist or validating their types. While this creates robustness issues rather than exploitable vulnerabilities, malformed work orders could cause AttributeError exceptions. Mitigation: Add defensive checks using getattr with defaults or validate work order structure.

No sanitization of user-controlled strings: Anchor paths and other work order fields are directly interpolated into packet output (quality.py:142, design.py output). While the output format is markdown (not HTML), malicious content in these fields could include misleading information or control characters. Mitigation: Consider basic sanitization of paths and strings used in output, especially if packet content could be rendered in contexts beyond plain text.
